title: Rivers (Early Goal-Directed Therapy)
reference: Rivers E et al., 2001, N Engl J Med [750, 809]
the_hook: The foundational trial that normalized aggressive, protocol-driven resuscitation for patients in severe sepsis and septic shock during their 'golden hours' [750, 808, 905].
if_consultant_asks: Rivers demonstrated that early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) targeting central venous pressure (8-12 mmHg), mean arterial pressure (>=65 mmHg), urine output (>=0.5 mL/kg/hr), and central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2 >=70%) within the first 6 hours of ED presentation significantly reduces in-hospital mortality compared to standard care [907, 908]. However, subsequent multicenter trials showed that the rigid, invasive elements of the protocol are not superior to high-quality usual care [730, 750].
killer_stat: In-hospital mortality was significantly reduced from 46.5% in the standard therapy group to 30.5% in the EGDT group (absolute risk reduction of 16%, relative risk reduction of 34.4%, p=0.009) [750, 911].
shift_action: DO aggressively resuscitate septic shock early on shift with prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluid resuscitation, but DON'T routinely place central venous catheters solely to monitor continuous ScvO2 or central venous pressure targets [164, 730].

title: ProCESS
reference: Yealy DM et al., 2014, N Engl J Med [40, 750]
the_hook: The first of the major 'trio' of trials challenging the necessity of invasive central venous pressure and ScvO2 monitoring for septic shock [730, 750].
if_consultant_asks: ProCESS showed that protocol-based septic shock resuscitation—including invasive monitoring of central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) and central venous pressure (CVP)—does not improve 60-day survival compared to high-quality usual care. This trial dismantled the absolute requirement for invasive EGDT protocols globally [730, 750].
killer_stat: No statistical difference in 60-day in-hospital mortality between EGDT protocol care (21.0%), protocol-based standard care (18.2%), and usual care (18.9%) [173, 730].
shift_action: DON'T routinely place central lines solely for ScvO2 or CVP targets in septic shock [731]; DO focus instead on early broad-spectrum antibiotics, fluid volume expansion, and clinical markers of resuscitation [164].

title: ARISE
reference: Peake SL et al., 2014, N Engl J Med [129, 750]
the_hook: The Australasian multicenter trial validating that invasive early goal-directed therapy does not improve survival in patients presenting with early septic shock [146, 730].
if_consultant_asks: ARISE validated the findings of the ProCESS trial in an international cohort, demonstrating that early goal-directed therapy does not improve 90-day survival compared to usual care in patients presenting to the emergency department with early septic shock [146, 730].
killer_stat: 90-day all-cause mortality was 18.6% in the EGDT group vs 18.8% in the usual care group (p=0.90) [146, 730].
shift_action: DON'T implement complex, invasive EGDT resuscitation algorithms; DO prioritize prompt sepsis identification, early lactate clearance, and rapid source control [731, 737].

title: ProMISe
reference: Mouncey PR et al., 2015, N Engl J Med [148, 750, 831]
the_hook: The UK-based trial that completed the trilogy of trials proving that usual resuscitation care has evolved to render invasive EGDT protocols unnecessary [730, 750].
if_consultant_asks: ProMISe confirmed that protocolized EGDT does not improve 90-day survival compared to usual care, while significantly increasing the use of intensive care resources and advanced monitoring [750, 833]. This definitive UK multicenter trial solidified the clinical consensus against routine EGDT [730, 750].
killer_stat: 90-day all-cause mortality was 29.5% in the EGDT group vs 29.2% in the usual care group (p=0.90) [750].
shift_action: DO treat septic shock aggressively with early antibiotics and fluid volume expansion on shift, but DON'T routinely insert central lines for CVP or ScvO2 monitoring [164, 731].

title: CRASH-2
reference: Shakur H et al., 2010, The Lancet [183, 750]
the_hook: The landmark trial establishing the safe and highly effective use of early Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in trauma patients with significant hemorrhage [207, 208].
if_consultant_asks: CRASH-2 demonstrated that early administration of Tranexamic Acid significantly reduces all-cause mortality and death due to bleeding in trauma patients with significant hemorrhage [211]. However, the benefit is strictly time-dependent; TXA must be given within 3 hours of injury, as administration past 3 hours shows no benefit and potentially increases death due to bleeding [809].
killer_stat: Significant reduction in all-cause mortality from 16.0% in the placebo group to 14.5% in the TXA group (relative risk 0.91, p=0.0035) with no increase in vascular occlusive events [211].
shift_action: DO give 1g TXA over 10 minutes followed by a maintenance infusion of 1g over 8 hours as soon as possible on shift, but ONLY if the estimated time since injury is less than 3 hours [208, 809].

title: CRASH-3
reference: Roberts I et al., 2019, The Lancet [750, 822]
the_hook: The international trial evaluating whether Tranexamic Acid (TXA) improves mortality in patients presenting with acute traumatic brain injury (TBI) [750, 822].
if_consultant_asks: CRASH-3 demonstrated that administering TXA to patients with traumatic brain injury and a GCS <=12 within 3 hours of injury significantly reduces head injury deaths [750, 825]. The effect is particularly pronounced in patients with mild-to-moderate TBI, whereas patients with severe, non-reactive TBI show negligible benefit [750, 775].
killer_stat: Risk of head injury death at 28 days was significantly reduced in the mild-to-moderate TBI subgroup (relative risk 0.78, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.95) when treated within 3 hours [750].
shift_action: DO administer TXA (1g bolus + 1g over 8 hours) to patients presenting with acute mild-to-moderate traumatic brain injury within 3 hours of injury, but DON'T expect survival benefits in patients presenting with severe, fixed dilated pupils [750, 825].

title: NINDS (Tissue Plasminogen Activator for Acute Ischemic Stroke)
reference: NINDS Study Group, 1995, N Engl J Med [750, 808]
the_hook: The foundational trial that established the benefit of intravenous recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA) in acute ischemic stroke within 3 hours [750, 808].
if_consultant_asks: NINDS proved that treatment with intravenous t-PA within 3 hours of ischemic stroke onset significantly improves the odds of a favorable functional outcome (minimal or no disability) at 3 months, despite a well-known risk of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage [750, 808].
killer_stat: A 12% absolute increase in patients achieving minimal or no disability at 3 months (p=0.008), despite a 6.4% rate of symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage in the t-PA group vs 0.6% in the placebo group [750].
shift_action: DO activate stroke protocols rapidly to deliver intravenous t-PA within the strict 3-hour window for eligible acute ischemic stroke patients on shift [750, 808].

title: ECASS-III
reference: Hacke W et al., 2008, N Engl J Med [657, 750]
the_hook: The landmark trial that safely expanded the therapeutic window for intravenous alteplase in acute ischemic stroke from 3 to 4.5 hours [657, 750].
if_consultant_asks: ECASS-III showed that administering recombinant t-PA between 3 and 4.5 hours after the onset of stroke symptoms significantly improves functional outcomes at 90 days compared to placebo [657, 750]. While it increases the risk of intracranial hemorrhage, it does not alter overall mortality [657].
killer_stat: Favorable neurological outcome (mRS 0-1) was significantly higher in the alteplase group at 90 days (52.4% vs 45.2%, odds ratio 1.34, p=0.04) [657, 750].
shift_action: DO administer intravenous alteplase to eligible acute ischemic stroke patients presenting within the 3 to 4.5-hour window on shift, keeping in mind the increased specificity of eligibility criteria for this late window [657].

title: PARAMEDIC-2
reference: Perkins GD et al., 2018, N Engl J Med [39, 750]
the_hook: The definitive prehospital trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of epinephrine in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) [730, 750].
if_consultant_asks: PARAMEDIC-2 proved that while epinephrine significantly improves return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and 30-day survival, it does not improve favorable neurological survival [730, 868]. Epinephrine-treated survivors are significantly more likely to suffer from severe neurological disability (Modified Rankin Scale score 4-5) compared to those receiving placebo [730].
killer_stat: 30-day survival was 3.2% in the epinephrine group vs 2.4% in the placebo group, but severe neurological impairment among survivors was 31.0% in the epinephrine group vs 17.8% in the placebo group [730].
shift_action: DO administer 1mg epinephrine per ACLS protocol during resuscitation to achieve ROSC, but DON'T over-promise functional recovery; utilize this data for realistic prognosis discussions with families regarding neurological outcomes [730, 868].

title: ARMA (Low Tidal Volume Ventilation)
reference: Brower RG et al., 2000, N Engl J Med [750, 808]
the_hook: The landmark ARDS Clinical Trials Network study establishing low tidal volume ventilation as the standard of care in acute respiratory distress syndrome [750, 808].
if_consultant_asks: ARMA demonstrated that mechanical ventilation utilizing a low tidal volume strategy (6 mL/kg of predicted body weight) significantly reduces mortality and ventilator-free days in patients with acute lung injury or ARDS compared to traditional high tidal volumes (12 mL/kg) [750, 808].
killer_stat: In-hospital mortality was reduced from 39.8% in the traditional tidal volume group to 31.0% in the low tidal volume group (p=0.007) [750].
shift_action: DO calculate the patient's predicted body weight (NOT actual weight) and set the initial ventilator tidal volume to 6 mL/kg for all patients with ARDS or acute lung injury on shift [750, 808].

title: PROSEVA
reference: Guérin C et al., 2013, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The definitive clinical trial proving that early, prolonged prone positioning dramatically improves survival in severe ARDS [670, 750].
if_consultant_asks: PROSEVA demonstrated that in patients with severe ARDS (defined as a PaO2:FiO2 ratio <150), early and prolonged prone-positioning sessions of at least 16 hours significantly reduce 28-day and 90-day mortality compared to remaining supine [670, 750].
killer_stat: 28-day mortality was halved from 32.8% in the supine group to 16.0% in the prone-positioning group (relative risk 0.44, p<0.001) [750].
shift_action: DO coordinate with the ICU team to initiate early prone positioning for patients with severe ARDS (PaO2:FiO2 <150) who require mechanical ventilation on shift [670, 750].

title: TTM (Targeted Temperature Management)
reference: Nielsen N et al., 2013, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The trial that challenged the necessity of cooling post-cardiac arrest survivors to 33°C by showing no benefit over 36°C [750].
if_consultant_asks: TTM showed that targeting a temperature of 33°C after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac cause does not provide any survival or neurological benefit compared to a target of 36°C [750].
killer_stat: No statistical difference in all-cause mortality at 180 days (50% in the 33°C group vs 48% in the 36°C group, p=0.51) or in favorable neurological outcomes [750].
shift_action: DON'T aggressively cool post-arrest patients down to 33°C as standard of care; DO focus on strict targeted normothermia (avoiding fever) on shift [750].

title: TTM2
reference: Dankiewicz J et al., 2021, N Engl J Med [750, 746]
the_hook: The large-scale trial confirming that targeted hypothermia does not improve outcomes compared to targeted normothermia in post-cardiac arrest survivors [750, 746].
if_consultant_asks: TTM2 demonstrated that therapeutic hypothermia at 33°C does not reduce 6-month mortality or improve functional recovery in coma survivors of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest compared to targeted normothermia (early fever prevention, maintaining temperature <=37.8°C) [750].
killer_stat: 6-month mortality was 57% in the hypothermia group vs 48% in the normothermia group, showing no benefit for active cooling to 33°C, while hypothermia was associated with more arrhythmias [750].
shift_action: DON'T routinely initiate active hypothermia protocols targeting 33°C on shift; DO focus on strictly preventing fever and keeping the patient's temperature <=37.8°C [750].

title: REVERT
reference: Appelboam A et al., 2015, The Lancet [201, 750]
the_hook: The highly practical trial evaluating a postural modification to the standard Valsalva maneuver for the treatment of supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) [201, 750].
if_consultant_asks: REVERT proved that a modified Valsalva maneuver—performing a standard strain in a semi-recumbent position, followed immediately by lying flat and raising the legs to 45 degrees for 15 seconds—is dramatically superior to the standard maneuver at restoring sinus rhythm [201, 750].
killer_stat: Conversion rate to sinus rhythm increased from 17% in the standard Valsalva group to 43% in the modified Valsalva group (absolute difference 26%, NNT=3, p<0.0001) [750].
shift_action: DO perform the modified Valsalva maneuver (passive leg raise flat on back after straining) as your first-line intervention for stable SVT on shift before reaching for adenosine [201, 750].

title: FEAST
reference: Maitland K et al., 2011, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The landmark African pediatric trial that shocked the medical world by proving that fluid boluses increase mortality in children with severe febrile illness and impaired perfusion [750].
if_consultant_asks: FEAST demonstrated that administering rapid fluid boluses (either albumin or normal saline) to febrile children with shock in resource-limited settings significantly increases 48-hour and 4-week mortality compared to no bolus [750]. This trial forced a global re-evaluation of aggressive fluid resuscitation in pediatric sepsis [750].
killer_stat: 48-hour mortality was significantly higher in the bolus groups (10.6% saline, 10.6% albumin) compared to the non-bolus control group (7.3%, p=0.01) [750].
shift_action: DON'T routinely administer aggressive, rapid fluid boluses to pediatric sepsis patients presenting with fever and mild-to-moderate perfusion impairment; DO proceed with highly cautious, titrated volume expansion on shift [750].

title: AIRWAYS-2
reference: Benger JR et al., 2018, JAMA [135, 750]
the_hook: The massive prehospital trial comparing a strategy of initial supraglottic airway (SGA) device insertion vs endotracheal intubation (ETI) in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [135, 750].
if_consultant_asks: AIRWAYS-2 showed that an initial prehospital airway management strategy utilizing a supraglottic airway device does not result in a significant difference in favorable neurological outcomes at 30 days compared to a strategy of tracheal intubation [750]. Paramedics often deviated from ETI due to technical difficulty [135].
killer_stat: Neurologically favorable survival (mRS 0-3) at 30 days or discharge was 6.4% in the SGA group vs 6.8% in the ETI group (no statistical difference, p=0.45) [750].
shift_action: DO utilize supraglottic airway devices as a primary, rapid airway strategy in the prehospital or early resuscitation phase of cardiac arrest on shift [750].

title: PART (Pragmatic Airway Resuscitation Trial)
reference: Wang HE et al., 2018, JAMA [152, 750]
the_hook: The pragmatic clinical trial comparing laryngeal tube (LT) insertion against endotracheal intubation (ETI) in adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [152, 750].
if_consultant_asks: PART demonstrated that a prehospital airway management strategy of initial laryngeal tube insertion (a supraglottic airway) results in significantly better 72-hour survival and hospital discharge compared to an initial strategy of endotracheal intubation [750].
killer_stat: 72-hour survival was significantly higher in the laryngeal tube group (18.3%) compared to the endotracheal intubation group (15.4%, absolute difference 2.9%, p=0.01) [750].
shift_action: DO adopt a supraglottic airway-first strategy in prehospital resuscitation protocols to maximize 72-hour survival and ROSC rates [750].

title: ADJUST-PE
reference: Righini M et al., 2014, JAMA [623, 750]
the_hook: The definitive trial validating the safety of an age-adjusted D-dimer threshold to rule out pulmonary embolism in older emergency department patients [632, 750].
if_consultant_asks: ADJUST-PE demonstrated that utilizing an age-adjusted D-dimer cutoff (Age x 10 in ug/L) for patients >50 years old with a low or intermediate pretest probability of PE safely excludes the diagnosis, significantly increasing the specificity of the assay and reducing unnecessary imaging [632, 755].
killer_stat: The 3-month failure rate (subsequent VTE) in patients ruled out using the age-adjusted threshold was only 0.3% (95% CI 0.1% to 1.0%), while reducing CT angiography scans by up to 20% [632, 755].
shift_action: DO calculate the age-adjusted D-dimer threshold (Age x 10 ug/L) for all patients older than 50 with a low-to-intermediate pretest probability of PE on shift, and DON'T order a CT angiogram if the result is below this adjusted cutoff [632, 755].

title: PROPPR
reference: Holcomb JB et al., 2015, JAMA [750]
the_hook: The randomized trial evaluating whether a 1:1:1 ratio of platelets, plasma, and red blood cells improves survival in severely hemorrhaging trauma patients compared to a 1:1:2 ratio [750].
if_consultant_asks: PROPPR showed that while there is no significant difference in overall 24-hour or 30-day mortality between a 1:1:1 ratio of platelets, plasma, and packed red blood cells and a 1:1:2 ratio, patients in the 1:1:1 group achieve significantly better early hemostasis and are less likely to die from exsanguination within the first 24 hours [750].
killer_stat: No statistical difference in 30-day mortality (22.4% in 1:1:1 vs 24.0% in 1:1:2), but significantly fewer deaths due to bleeding in the first 24 hours in the 1:1:1 group (9.2% vs 14.6%, p=0.03) [750].
shift_action: DO activate your hospital's massive transfusion protocol utilizing a 1:1:1 balanced ratio (platelets:plasma:PRBCs) for severely hemorrhaging trauma patients on shift [750].

title: PAMPer
reference: Sperry JL et al., 2018, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The landmark prehospital trial proving that administering thawed plasma during air medical transport reduces mortality in trauma patients at risk for hemorrhagic shock [706, 750].
if_consultant_asks: PAMPer proved that the prehospital administration of 2 units of thawed plasma to trauma patients at risk for hemorrhagic shock significantly reduces 30-day mortality and the requirement for post-hospital blood transfusions compared to standard care [750].
killer_stat: 30-day mortality was significantly reduced from 33.0% in the standard-care group to 23.2% in the prehospital plasma group (absolute risk reduction of 9.8%, p=0.002) [750].
shift_action: DO advocate for the early administration of thawed plasma in prehospital or early trauma resuscitation algorithms to prevent mortality from hemorrhagic shock on shift [750].

title: Villanueva (Restrictive vs. Liberal Transfusion in UGIB)
reference: Villanueva C et al., 2013, N Engl J Med [750, 813]
the_hook: The seminal trial establishing restrictive blood transfusion strategies as the gold standard in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) [750].
if_consultant_asks: Villanueva proved that a restrictive transfusion strategy (transfusing only when hemoglobin drops <7 g/dL, targeting 7-9 g/dL) significantly improves 45-day survival in acute UGIB compared to a liberal strategy (transfusing when Hb drops <9 g/dL), while also reducing rebleeding rates and complications [750, 813].
killer_stat: 45-day survival was significantly higher in the restrictive group compared to the liberal group (95% vs 91%, p=0.02) [750].
shift_action: DON'T transfuse packed red blood cells in stable patients with acute upper GI bleeding unless their hemoglobin is less than 7 g/dL on shift, unless severe cardiovascular co-morbidities exist [750].

title: NoPAC
reference: Stevens JW et al., 2021, The Lancet [750]
the_hook: The multicenter trial evaluating the utility of topical Tranexamic Acid (TXA) in patients presenting with persistent epistaxis [750].
if_consultant_asks: NoPAC demonstrated that the application of topical Tranexamic Acid (either on a soaked cotton pledget or gauze) does not reduce the need for anterior nasal packing in patients with persistent epistaxis compared to placebo [750].
killer_stat: There was no difference in the rate of anterior nasal packing required between the TXA group (43.7%) and the placebo group (41.3%, p=0.53) [750].
shift_action: DON'T rely on topical TXA as a silver bullet for persistent epistaxis; DO proceed with standard compression, vasoconstrictors, and mechanical packing if standard pressure fails [750].

title: INTERACT2
reference: Anderson CS et al., 2013, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The large-scale trial evaluating intensive blood pressure lowering in patients presenting with acute intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) [750].
if_consultant_asks: INTERACT2 showed that while intensive blood pressure lowering (targeting systolic BP <140 mmHg within 1 hour) does not significantly reduce 90-day death or severe disability compared to standard guidelines (<180 mmHg), it is safe and results in significantly better functional recovery on ordinal mRS shift analysis [750].
killer_stat: No statistical difference in the primary composite endpoint of death or major disability (relative risk 0.95, p=0.10), but a significant shift toward better functional outcomes (lower mRS scores) in the intensive treatment group (p=0.04) [750].
shift_action: DO initiate rapid, titrated intravenous antihypertensive therapy (e.g., clevidipine or nicardipine) to target a SBP <140 mmHg in patients presenting with acute intracerebral hemorrhage on shift [750].

title: PATCH (Platelet Transfusion in Cerebral Haemorrhage)
reference: Baharoglu MI et al., 2016, The Lancet [750]
the_hook: The trial that reversed standard practice by proving that platelet transfusions increase death and disability in patients with intracerebral hemorrhage who are on antiplatelet therapy [750].
if_consultant_asks: PATCH demonstrated that administering platelet transfusions to patients with acute spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage who were taking antiplatelet therapy within 6 hours of symptom onset significantly increases the odds of death or severe disability at 3 months compared to standard care [750].
killer_stat: Odds of death or severe disability (mRS 4-6) at 3 months were significantly higher in the platelet transfusion group compared to standard care (adjusted odds ratio 2.05, p=0.011) [750].
shift_action: DON'T routinely administer platelet transfusions on shift to patients presenting with intracranial hemorrhage solely because they were taking aspirin or clopidogrel [750].

title: ARREST (Advanced Reperfusion Strategies for Refractory Cardiac Arrest)
reference: Yannopoulos D et al., 2020, The Lancet [61, 750]
the_hook: The single-center trial demonstrating the overwhelming efficacy of early Extracorporeal CPR (ECPR) for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest with shockable rhythms [61, 750].
if_consultant_asks: ARREST proved that in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and refractory ventricular fibrillation (no ROSC after 3 shocks), early transfer to an ECMO-capable center for cannulatory ECPR results in dramatically higher survival to hospital discharge compared to standard prehospital ACLS resuscitation [61, 750].
killer_stat: The trial was halted early for efficacy: survival to discharge with favorable neurological recovery was 43% in the ECPR group compared to just 7% in the standard ACLS group (p=0.006) [750].
shift_action: DO advocate for rapid transport and ECPR activation for patients with refractory shockable out-of-hospital cardiac arrest if a local, highly-experienced ECPR pathway is available [750].

title: INCEPTION
reference: Hoedemaekers et al., 2023, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The multicenter trial evaluating whether early ECPR improves neurological survival in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest compared to conventional CPR [750].
if_consultant_asks: INCEPTION showed that in a pragmatic, multicenter real-world setting, a strategy of early ECPR for refractory OHCA does not result in a statistically significant improvement in neurologically favorable survival at 30 days compared to high-quality conventional CPR [750].
killer_stat: Favorable neurological survival at 30 days was 20% in the ECPR group vs 16% in the conventional CPR group (odds ratio 1.4, p=0.52, no statistical difference) [750].
shift_action: DO consider ECPR in refractory cardiac arrest, but recognize that its clinical efficacy is highly dependent on restrictive patient selection, low door-to-ECMO times, and high operator volumes [77, 750].

title: SMART
reference: Semler MW et al., 2018, N Engl J Med [638, 750]
the_hook: The massive ICU trial demonstrating that balanced crystalloids reduce major adverse kidney events compared to normal saline [638, 750].
if_consultant_asks: SMART showed that in critically ill adults, the use of balanced crystalloids (Lactated Ringer's or Plasma-Lyte) for fluid resuscitation significantly reduces the composite endpoint of Major Adverse Kidney Events within 30 days (MAKE30) compared to using 0.9% normal saline [750, 758].
killer_stat: MAKE30 was significantly reduced from 15.4% in the saline group to 14.3% in the balanced crystalloid group (p=0.04) [750].
shift_action: DO choose balanced crystalloids (like Lactated Ringer's) over 0.9% normal saline as your primary resuscitation fluid for critically ill adults on shift, particularly to prevent hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis [750, 758].

title: SALT-ED
reference: Self WH et al., 2018, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The massive emergency department trial comparing balanced crystalloids against normal saline in non-critically ill patients [750].
if_consultant_asks: SALT-ED showed that among non-critically ill adults receiving intravenous fluids in the ED, the use of balanced crystalloids does not alter hospital-free days, but significantly reduces subsequent major adverse kidney events (MAKE30) [750].
killer_stat: No difference in hospital-free days, but a significant reduction in MAKE30 in the balanced crystalloids group (4.7% vs 5.6%, p=0.01) [750].
shift_action: DO default to balanced crystalloids (Lactated Ringer's) for routine intravenous fluid administration in the emergency department on shift [750].

title: ADRENAL
reference: Venkatesh B et al., 2018, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The large-scale trial evaluating whether continuous hydrocortisone infusion improves survival in patients with septic shock [750].
if_consultant_asks: ADRENAL demonstrated that in patients with septic shock undergoing mechanical ventilation, a continuous infusion of hydrocortisone (200 mg daily) does not reduce 90-day mortality compared to placebo [750]. However, it significantly accelerates shock reversal and reduces time on mechanical ventilation [750].
killer_stat: 90-day mortality was 27.9% in the hydrocortisone group vs 28.9% in the placebo group (no statistical difference, p=0.50), while median time to shock resolution was reduced from 4 to 3 days (p<0.001) [750].

title: APROCCHSS
reference: Annane D et al., 2018, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The multicenter trial proving that combined hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone therapy improves survival in severe septic shock [750].
if_consultant_asks: APROCCHSS showed that in patients with severe septic shock, the combination of hydrocortisone (50mg IV bolus every 6 hours) and oral fludrocortisone (50mcg daily) significantly reduces 90-day all-cause mortality and hastens vasopressor weaning compared to placebo [750].
killer_stat: 90-day all-cause mortality was significantly reduced from 48.9% in the placebo group to 43.0% in the steroid combination group (p=0.03) [750].
shift_action: DO initiate hydrocortisone (50mg IV q6h) plus oral fludrocortisone (50mcg daily) on shift for patients with refractory septic shock who require high-dose vasopressors [750].

title: PROMISE (Netherlands MR CLEAN/PROMISE)
reference: Berkhemer OA et al., 2015, N Engl J Med [126, 750]
the_hook: The landmark Dutch trial that proved the overwhelming efficacy of early endovascular thrombectomy for acute ischemic stroke due to proximal large vessel occlusion (LVO) [126, 750].
if_consultant_asks: PROMISE proved that intraarterial thrombectomy within 6 hours of stroke onset, in addition to standard medical care (including t-PA if eligible), significantly improves functional outcomes and rate of functional independence at 90 days in patients with a proximal LVO in the anterior circulation [126, 750].
killer_stat: The rate of functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days was significantly higher in the thrombectomy group (32.6%) compared to standard care alone (19.1%, absolute benefit of 13.5%, p<0.001) [126, 750].
shift_action: DO emergently activate the neurointerventional team and transfer patients with confirmed anterior circulation Large Vessel Occlusions for mechanical thrombectomy within 6 hours [750].

title: DAWN
reference: Nogueira RG et al., 2018, N Engl J Med [633, 750]
the_hook: The landmark neurological trial that shifted stroke protocols from a strict time-based window to a tissue-based mismatch window [633, 750].
if_consultant_asks: DAWN proved that mechanical thrombectomy performed between 6 and 24 hours last known well in patients with an anterior circulation Large Vessel Occlusion who have a clinical-core mismatch (severe deficit but small infarct core on perfusion imaging) significantly improves functional independence at 90 days [633, 750].
killer_stat: Functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days was achieved in 49% of patients in the thrombectomy group compared to just 13% in the control group (treatment effect of 36%, p<0.001) [633, 750].
shift_action: DO obtain advanced perfusion imaging (CT perfusion or MRI) for patients with acute stroke presenting late (6 to 24 hours), and DON'T deny thrombectomy solely based on time elapsed if a tissue-based clinical-core mismatch is present [633, 750].

title: OPALS (Ontario Prehospital Advanced Life Support Study)
reference: Stiell IG et al., 2004, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The massive system-wide trial proving that adding advanced life support (ALS) drugs and intubation to rapid defibrillation does not improve survival in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [750].
if_consultant_asks: OPALS demonstrated that the addition of prehospital advanced life support (including intubation and IV drugs) to an existing rapid-defibrillation program does not improve survival to hospital discharge in patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest [750].
killer_stat: Overall survival to discharge was virtually identical before (5.0%) and after (5.1%) the optimization of the advanced life support prehospital system (p=0.83) [750].
shift_action: DO prioritize rapid defibrillation and high-quality, uninterrupted chest compressions over complex prehospital advanced airway and drug interventions on shift [750].

title: SAFE
reference: SAFE Study Investigators, 2004, N Engl J Med [750, 661]
the_hook: The landmark trial comparing albumin against normal saline for fluid resuscitation in the intensive care setting [661, 750].
if_consultant_asks: SAFE demonstrated that the use of 4% albumin for fluid resuscitation in critically ill patients results in similar 28-day mortality compared to using 0.9% normal saline [750, 661]. However, a pre-specified subgroup analysis revealed significant harm (increased mortality) when albumin was used in patients with traumatic brain injury [750].
killer_stat: No overall difference in 28-day mortality (relative risk 0.99, p=0.87), but patients with traumatic brain injury randomized to receive albumin had significantly higher mortality (relative risk 1.62, p=0.009) [750].
shift_action: DON'T use albumin for fluid resuscitation in patients presenting with traumatic brain injury on shift; DO use normal saline or balanced crystalloids instead [750].

title: 6S
reference: Perner A et al., 2012, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The Scandinavian trial proving that hydroxyethyl starch (HES) increases mortality and renal replacement therapy in severe sepsis [750].
if_consultant_asks: 6S demonstrated that fluid resuscitation utilizing hydroxyethyl starch (HES 130/0.42) in patients with severe sepsis significantly increases 90-day mortality and the requirement for renal replacement therapy compared to Ringer's acetate [750].
killer_stat: 90-day mortality was significantly higher in the HES group compared to the Ringer's acetate group (51% vs 43%, relative risk 1.17, p=0.03) [750].
shift_action: DON'T utilize starches or synthetic colloid solutions for resuscitation in patients presenting with sepsis on shift [750].

title: CHEST
reference: Myburgh JA et al., 2012, N Engl J Med [750]
the_hook: The large-scale ICU trial confirming that hydroxyethyl starch (HES) increases kidney injury and renal replacement therapy compared to saline [750].
if_consultant_asks: CHEST proved that fluid resuscitation with hydroxyethyl starch (HES 130/0.4) does not reduce 90-day mortality in critically ill patients compared to normal saline, while significantly increasing the need for renal replacement therapy and causing severe adverse effects [750].
killer_stat: No difference in 90-day mortality (18.0% HES vs 17.0% saline), but a significant increase in the use of renal replacement therapy in the HES group (relative risk 1.21, p=0.04) [750].
shift_action: DON'T administer hydroxyethyl starch or other synthetic colloids for fluid resuscitation in the ED on shift [750].

title: NICE-SUGAR
reference: NICE-SUGAR Study Investigators, 2009, N Engl J Med [660, 750]
the_hook: The trial that safely de-implemented intensive insulin 'tight' glycemic control in the intensive care unit by proving it increases mortality [660, 750].
if_consultant_asks: NICE-SUGAR demonstrated that targeting a tight blood glucose range of 81-108 mg/dL in critically ill patients significantly increases 90-day mortality and the incidence of severe hypoglycemia compared to a conventional target of <=180 mg/dL [660, 750].
killer_stat: 90-day mortality was significantly higher in the intensive-control group (27.5% vs 24.9%, odds ratio 1.14, p=0.02) and severe hypoglycemia (<40 mg/dL) was drastically increased (6.8% vs 0.5%, p<0.001) [660, 750].
shift_action: DON'T target strict, tight blood glucose targets (e.g., <110 mg/dL) on shift; DO focus on keeping blood sugars <=180 mg/dL in critically ill resuscitations [660, 750].

title: ProCESS (Agitation)
reference: J Emerg Med, 2024 [750]
the_hook: The modern trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of intramuscular olanzapine vs haloperidol for acute agitation in the emergency department [750].
if_consultant_asks: This ProCESS sub-study demonstrated that intramuscular olanzapine is non-inferior to haloperidol in reducing acute agitation scores, while being associated with significantly fewer extrapyramidal and adverse side effects [750].
killer_stat: Olanzapine met non-inferiority criteria for agitation control with a statistically significant reduction in adverse event rates compared to haloperidol [750].
shift_action: DO consider intramuscular olanzapine as a preferred first-line atypical antipsychotic over haloperidol for the chemical restraint of stable, acutely agitated ED patients on shift [750].

title: CLASP (Collaborative Low-dose Aspirin Study in Pregnancy)
reference: CLASP Collaborative Group, 1994, The Lancet [646, 750]
the_hook: The landmark obstetric trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of low-dose aspirin for preeclampsia and fetal growth restriction [646, 750].
if_consultant_asks: CLASP demonstrated that while daily low-dose aspirin (60 mg) does not significantly reduce the overall incidence of preeclampsia, it safely reduces preterm delivery rates and is highly effective at preventing preeclampsia in the specific subgroup of women with early-onset or severe risk factors [646, 750].
killer_stat: No significant difference in overall preeclampsia rates, but a significant 12% relative reduction in preterm delivery (p=0.003) and FGR in high-risk patients [646].
shift_action: DO initiate low-dose aspirin on shift for pregnant patients identified as high risk for preeclampsia, keeping in mind the dose has evolved to 150 mg daily [647].

title: Ottawa Ankle Rules
reference: Stiell IG et al., 1992, BMJ / Wikipedia [37, 753, 761]
the_hook: The gold-standard clinical decision rule designed to safely rule out fractures and bypass radiographs in acute blunt ankle and foot injuries [139, 753].
if_consultant_asks: The Ottawa Ankle Rules allow clinical clearance of the ankle and midfoot without radiography if the patient has no bone tenderness at the posterior distal 6 cm of the lateral or medial malleolus, the base of the fifth metatarsal, or the navicular bone, AND can bear weight for 4 steps both immediately and in the ED [139, 753].
killer_stat: Demonstrated sensitivity of 98.5% to 100% for identifying clinically important fractures, safely reducing the rate of unnecessary ankle and foot radiographs by 14% to 36% [139, 753].
shift_action: DO apply the Ottawa Ankle Rules explicitly on shift to clinically clear stable ankle sprains and defer unnecessary foot or ankle X-rays [139, 753].

title: Ottawa Knee Rules
reference: Stiell IG et al., 1995, JAMA / Wikipedia [699, 753]
the_hook: The clinical prediction pathway to safely exclude knee fractures and avoid unnecessary radiography following acute blunt knee injuries [753, 796].
if_consultant_asks: The Ottawa Knee Rules state that a knee radiograph is only required if the patient has acute blunt knee trauma and any of: 1) age >=55 years; 2) isolated tenderness of the patella; 3) tenderness of the fibular head; 4) inability to flex the knee to 90 degrees; or 5) inability to bear weight for 4 steps both immediately and in the ED [753, 798].
killer_stat: Achieves a sensitivity of 98% to 100% for detecting knee fractures, reducing the rate of knee radiographs by approximately 26% to 28% [753, 798].
shift_action: DO apply the Ottawa Knee Rules to clinically clear minor blunt knee trauma on shift without ordering knee films [753, 798].

title: Canadian CT Head Rule
reference: Stiell IG et al., 2001, The Lancet [628, 753]
the_hook: The definitive clinical decision rule to safely rule out intracranial injuries requiring neurosurgical intervention in patients with minor head trauma (GCS 13-15) [627, 628, 753].
if_consultant_asks: The Canadian CT Head Rule identifies alert and stable patients with minor head injury who can safely defer cranial imaging if they meet no high-risk criteria (GCS <15 at 2 hours, suspected open/depressed fracture, basilar fracture signs, >=2 episodes of vomiting, age >=65) and no medium-risk criteria (retrograde amnesia >=30 min, dangerous mechanism) [628, 753].
killer_stat: Achieves 100% sensitivity for identifying patients requiring neurosurgical intervention, reducing unnecessary ED head CT scan rates by nearly one-third [628, 753].
shift_action: DO apply the Canadian CT Head Rule to clinically clear minor head injuries on shift and safely avoid cranial radiation [628, 753].

title: PECARN Pediatric Head Trauma Rules
reference: Kuppermann N et al., 2009, The Lancet [629, 753]
the_hook: The gold-standard pediatric head injury framework used to safely rule out Clinically Important Traumatic Brain Injury (ciTBI) and avoid unnecessary CT radiation [627, 629].
if_consultant_asks: PECARN stratifies pediatric blunt head trauma into age-specific frameworks (<2 y and >=2 y) [629]. Children with a normal mental status, no palpable/basilar skull fractures, no loss of consciousness (or <5s), no severe mechanism, and no severe headache/vomiting are at negligible risk and require no head CT [629, 753].
killer_stat: Negative predictive value of 99.95% for clinically important brain injuries in children under 2 years old, safely sparing countless pediatric patients from unnecessary CT scans [629, 753].
shift_action: DO apply the age-specific PECARN head trauma rules on shift before ordering head CT scans on pediatric head injuries [629, 753].

title: NEXUS C-Spine Rule
reference: Hoffman JR et al., 2000, N Engl J Med [636, 753]
the_hook: The widely validated, simple bedside rule to clinically clear the cervical spine in stable blunt trauma patients without radiography [627, 753].
if_consultant_asks: The NEXUS rule states that a blunt trauma patient can be clinically cleared of C-spine injury without radiographic imaging if they meet all 5 low-risk criteria: 1) no midline cervical tenderness; 2) no focal neurological deficit; 3) normal level of alertness; 4) no evidence of intoxication; and 5) no painful distracting injuries [753, 779].
killer_stat: Sensitivity of 99.6% to 99.8% for ruling out clinically important cervical spine injuries, allowing rapid bedside clearance without imaging [753, 772].
shift_action: DO utilize the NEXUS criteria as a rapid bedside screening tool to clear the neck of stable trauma patients on shift [753].

title: Canadian C-Spine Rule
reference: Stiell IG et al., 2001, JAMA [753, 788]
the_hook: The highly structured, superiorly specific decision rule to clear the cervical spine in stable blunt trauma patients [753, 770].
if_consultant_asks: The Canadian C-Spine Rule uses a 3-step algorithm: 1) identifies high-risk factors mandating imaging (age >=65, dangerous mechanism, paresthesias); 2) identifies low-risk factors allowing safe assessment of range of motion (sitting in ED, ambulatory since injury, delayed neck pain, no midline tenderness); and 3) requires the patient to actively rotate their neck 45° bilaterally [753, 770].
killer_stat: Achieves a sensitivity of 100% for detecting clinically important C-spine injuries with a superior specificity (42.5%) to NEXUS (12.9%), significantly reducing radiography rates [753, 770].
shift_action: DO prioritize the Canadian C-Spine Rule over NEXUS for clearing the cervical spine in stable trauma patients on shift to safely reduce unnecessary X-rays [753, 779].

title: Wells' Criteria for Deep Vein Thrombosis
reference: Wells PS et al., 2003, N Engl J Med [623, 755]
the_hook: The widely accepted clinical prediction score used to convert physical findings into a standardized pre-test probability of lower-extremity DVT [754, 882].
if_consultant_asks: The Wells' Criteria for DVT stratify patients into low (score <=0), moderate (1-2), and high (>=3) risk categories, or simplified likely (>=2) vs unlikely (<=1) cohorts [872, 886]. Resuscitation pathways dictate combining unlikely risk with a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer to safely rule out DVT without imaging [872, 887].
killer_stat: Negative predictive value of >99% when a low-pretest probability (Wells unlikely) is paired with a negative moderate- or high-sensitivity D-dimer [872].
shift_action: DO document a Wells' DVT score explicitly before ordering a D-dimer or compression ultrasound for suspected deep vein thrombosis on shift [872, 889].

title: Wells' Criteria for Pulmonary Embolism
reference: van Belle A et al., 2006, JAMA [214, 755]
the_hook: The gold-standard risk-stratification model used to objectify the pretest probability of acute pulmonary embolism [754, 840].
if_consultant_asks: The Wells' PE criteria utilize a weighted scoring system (DVT signs, HR >100, immobilization, prior VTE, hemoptysis, malignancy, alternative diagnosis less likely) [865]. A score <=4 ('PE unlikely') directs workup to a D-dimer, whereas a score >4 ('PE likely') dictates bypassing D-dimer and proceeding directly to CT angiography [846, 865].
killer_stat: Patients determined to have a low pre-test probability (0-1 points) have a PE prevalence of only 1.3%, allowing safe D-dimer clearance [845, 847].
shift_action: DO apply the two-tier Wells' PE score (likely vs unlikely) in conjunction with a high-sensitivity D-dimer on shift to safely exclude pulmonary embolism [846, 852].

title: PERC Rule (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria)
reference: Kline JA et al., 2004, J Thromb Haemost [637, 755]
the_hook: The bedside rule designed to safely rule out pulmonary embolism in low-risk patients without even ordering a D-dimer [627, 755].
if_consultant_asks: The PERC rule utilizes 8 clinical criteria (age <50, HR <100, SaO2 >=95%, no unilateral leg swelling, no hemoptysis, no hormone use, no prior VTE, no recent trauma/surgery) [755]. In patients with low clinical gestalt (pre-test probability <15%), if all 8 PERC criteria are negative, PE is ruled out with no further testing needed [4, 627].
killer_stat: Reduces the post-test probability of pulmonary embolism to <1% in low-gestalt cohorts without a D-dimer, avoiding false positives and unnecessary downstream imaging [755].
shift_action: DO apply the PERC rule to stable, low-gestalt chest pain or shortness of breath patients on shift, and DON'T order a D-dimer if they are 'PERC-negative' [4, 755].

title: HEART Score Validation
reference: Backus BE et al., 2013, Int J Cardiol [631, 755]
the_hook: The seminal clinical decision tool used to risk-stratify ED chest pain patients and safely identify low-risk cohorts for early discharge [631, 755].
if_consultant_asks: The HEART Score evaluates History, ECG, Age, Risk factors, and Troponin (0-2 points each) [631, 755]. Patients with a score of 0-3 and a negative initial troponin have a very low risk of Major Adverse Cardiac Events (MACE) and can be safely discharged from the ED [10, 755].
killer_stat: 6-week risk of MACE was only 1.7% in patients with a HEART score of 0-3, safely identifying a massive cohort of patients suitable for early discharge [631, 755].
shift_action: DO calculate the HEART score for all patients presenting to the ED with possible acute coronary syndrome, and use a score of 0-3 with negative troponin to safely discharge the patient [10, 755].

title: ADAPT Trial (2-Hour Accelerated Diagnostic Protocol)
reference: Than M et al., 2012 / 2014, J Am Coll Cardiol / JAMA Intern Med [14, 25, 756]
the_hook: The randomized clinical trial validating a 2-hour accelerated diagnostic protocol for low-risk chest pain [14, 756].
if_consultant_asks: ADAPT proved that a chest pain protocol utilizing a modified TIMI score of 0, negative troponins at 0 and 2 hours, and a normal ECG can safely identify low-risk patients suitable for early discharge from the ED [14, 15, 756].
killer_stat: ED discharge rates within 6 hours significantly increased from 11.0% in standard care to 19.3% in the ADAPT pathway (p=0.008) with a 100% negative predictive value for MACE [756].
shift_action: DO initiate a rapid 0/2-hour troponin protocol on shift for low-risk chest pain patients who are ECG-negative with a modified TIMI score of 0 [14, 15, 756].

title: HINTS Bedside Oculomotor Exam
reference: Newman-Toker DE et al., 2009, Stroke [137, 757]
the_hook: The three-step bedside oculomotor examination used to differentiate central stroke from peripheral vestibular neuritis in acute vestibular syndrome [757].
if_consultant_asks: The HINTS exam evaluates three signs: horizontal Head Impulse test (normal in central stroke), Nystagmus (direction-changing horizontal nystagmus is central), and Test of Skew (vertical ocular misalignment is central) [757]. Any single central sign indicates a central stroke [137, 757].
killer_stat: Bedside HINTS exam is 100% sensitive and 96% specific for central stroke, outperforming early diffusion-weighted MRI (DWI) within the first 24-48 hours [137, 757].
shift_action: DO perform a complete HINTS exam on shift for patients presenting with continuous acute vestibular syndrome (constant vertigo, nystagmus, nausea) before ordering an early MRI [757].

title: Ottawa SAH Rule
reference: Perry JJ et al., 2013, JAMA [742, 757]
the_hook: The highly sensitive bedside tool developed to identify which patients with acute non-traumatic headaches require cranial imaging to rule out subarachnoid hemorrhage [725, 757].
if_consultant_asks: The Ottawa SAH Rule clears neurologically intact patients presenting with acute headache peaking within 1 hour if they have: age <40, no neck pain/stiffness, no witnessed loss of consciousness, no onset during exertion, no thunderclap onset, and normal neck flexion [729, 757].
killer_stat: Achieves a sensitivity of 100% for detecting SAH with a specificity of 13.6% to 22%, safely ruling out subarachnoid hemorrhage when negative [726, 757].
shift_action: DO utilize the Ottawa SAH Rule to guide head CT decisions on shift for alert patients with sudden onset 'thunderclap' headaches [727, 757].

title: PECARN Pediatric Abdominal Trauma Rule
reference: Holmes JF et al., 2013 / 2024, Annals of Emerg Med / Lancet Child Adolesc Health [689, 705, 760]
the_hook: The clinical decision rule used to identify children at negligible risk for intra-abdominal injury (IAI) requiring intervention following blunt torso trauma [705, 760].
if_consultant_asks: The PECARN Abdominal Trauma Rule clears pediatric blunt trauma patients from requiring abdominal CT if they have: no altered mental status, no abdominal wall trauma/bruising, no abdominal tenderness, no thoracic trauma, no abdominal pain, no vomiting, and normal breath sounds [760].
killer_stat: Achieves a negative predictive value of 99.8% for intra-abdominal injuries requiring acute intervention, safely sparing low-risk children from abdominal radiation [760].
shift_action: DO apply the PECARN abdominal trauma rule explicitly on shift to safely defer abdominal CT scans in stable pediatric trauma [760].

title: Bacterial Meningitis Score (BMS) for Children
reference: Nigrovic LE et al., 2002 / 2007, Pediatrics / JAMA [67, 760]
the_hook: The validated clinical prediction rule designed to distinguish bacterial from aseptic meningitis in children presenting with CSF pleocytosis [112, 760].
if_consultant_asks: The BMS assigns points based on: positive CSF Gram stain (+2), CSF absolute neutrophil count (ANC) >=1000 cells/uL (+1), CSF protein >=80 mg/dL (+1), blood ANC >=10,000 cells/uL (+1), and seizure at presentation (+1) [66, 111]. A score of 0 indicates aseptic meningitis is highly likely, allowing outpatient management [67, 110, 760].
killer_stat: A score of 0 has a 100% negative predictive value and 73% specificity for ruling out bacterial meningitis, safely reducing unnecessary hospital admissions [673, 760].
shift_action: DO calculate the BMS for pediatric patients presenting on shift with CSF pleocytosis, and DO consider outpatient management if the score is 0 and they have had no pre-LP antibiotics [67, 760].

title: SNAP Acetaminophen Regimen
reference: EClinicalMedicine, 2019 [714, 760]
the_hook: The simplified 12-hour, two-bag acetylcysteine protocol that significantly limits systemic adverse reactions in acetaminophen overdose [58, 760].
if_consultant_asks: The SNAP protocol replaces the complex, standard 21-hour Prescott protocol with a 12-hour regimen: 100 mg/kg over 2 hours followed by 200 mg/kg over 10 hours [760]. It results in a dramatic reduction in non-allergic anaphylactoid reactions and shortens overall hospital stay [760].
killer_stat: Equivalent efficacy in preventing hepatotoxicity compared to standard 3-bag regimens, while reducing anaphylactoid reaction rates from ~20% down to ~5% [760].
shift_action: DO initiate the SNAP 12-hour acetylcysteine regimen for acute acetaminophen overdoses on shift to avoid infusion-related hypersensitivity reactions and shorten hospital stays [760].

title: Black Widow Antivenom Clinical Trial
reference: EM Lit of Note [760]
the_hook: The clinical trial challenging the routine use of expensive antivenom for clinically significant latrodectism [760].
if_consultant_asks: This toxicological trial demonstrated that administering black widow antivenom to patients with acute severe pain refractory to standard analgesics does not significantly reduce persistent pain or treatment failure compared to placebo [760].
killer_stat: The antivenom cohort had high rates of persistent pain and treatment failure, while the placebo group showed substantial, comparable recovery at a fraction of the medical cost [760].
shift_action: DON'T routinely administer expensive black widow antivenom for latrodectism on shift; DO prioritize aggressive, high-quality supportive care and standard analgesics [760].

title: San Francisco Syncope Rule
reference: Quinn J et al., 2006, Annals of Emerg Med [9, 811]
the_hook: The historical clinical decision rule designed to predict serious 30-day outcomes in patients presenting with acute syncope [9, 811].
if_consultant_asks: The San Francisco Syncope Rule utilizes the CHESS mnemonic: History of Congestive heart failure, Hematocrit <30%, abnormal ECG, History of Shortness of breath, and Systolic BP <90 mmHg [9]. If any one is present, the patient is high risk for serious 30-day outcomes [9].
killer_stat: Initially derived with high sensitivity to safely reduce syncope admissions by nearly 25%, but subsequent external validation studies demonstrated significantly lower diagnostic performance [9].
shift_action: DON'T rely on the San Francisco Syncope Rule in isolation to clear syncopal patients on shift; DO combine structured risk factors with clinical gestalt [9].

title: LRINEC Score
reference: JournalFeed Landmark Summaries [8]
the_hook: The laboratory risk indicator score developed to differentiate ordinary soft-tissue infections from necrotizing fasciitis [8].
if_consultant_asks: The LRINEC score assigns points based on CRP, WBC, Hemoglobin, Sodium, Creatinine, and Glucose [8]. A score >=6 is considered suspicious for necrotizing fasciitis [8]. However, subsequent large-scale clinical studies have called its diagnostic accuracy into question [8].
killer_stat: Initially touted with high diagnostic utility, subsequent studies demonstrated high false-negative rates, proving that a low LRINEC score cannot safely rule out early necrotizing soft-tissue infection [8].
shift_action: DON'T utilize a low LRINEC score to clinically rule out necrotizing fasciitis on shift if physical exam signs (crepitus, pain out of proportion, rapid progression) are concerning [8].

title: Sgarbossa Criteria
reference: JournalFeed Landmark Summaries [9]
the_hook: The classic ECG criteria used to diagnose acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) in the presence of a Left Bundle Branch Block (LBBB) [9].
if_consultant_asks: The Sgarbossa criteria evaluate three ECG signs: 1) concordant ST elevation >=1 mm in any lead (+5 points); 2) concordant ST depression >=1 mm in V1-V3 (+3 points); and 3) discordant ST elevation >=5 mm (+2 points) [9]. A score >=3 indicates high specificity for acute MI [9].
killer_stat: Concordant ST elevation >=1 mm has a specificity of over 98% for identifying acute myocardial infarction in the setting of LBBB [9].
shift_action: DO emergently activate the cardiac catheterization lab on shift if a patient with LBBB presents with ischemic chest pain and concordant ST changes matching Sgarbossa criteria [9].

title: CURB-65 / CRB-65
reference: 2 Minute Medicine Classics / Thorax 2003 [4, 661]
the_hook: The widely used clinical prediction score designed to risk-stratify 30-day mortality in community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) [4, 661].
if_consultant_asks: CURB-65 assigns 1 point for each of: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate >=30/min, low Blood pressure (SBP <90 or DBP <=60), and age >=65 years [661]. A score of 0-1 suggests outpatient care is safe; a score >=3 suggests severe pneumonia requiring inpatient admission or intensive care [661].
killer_stat: Patients with a score >=3 have a 30-day mortality rate exceeding 19%, identifying a high-risk cohort requiring prompt aggressive therapy [661].
shift_action: DO utilize CURB-65 (or CRB-65 if lab values are pending) to objective-stratify mortality risk and guide admission vs discharge decisions for pneumonia on shift [4, 661].
